_comment: Dialogue rules. (1) Every answer that matters is a `check` against the journal, never a menu pick - you can always say the words, they only WORK at enough reliability, and the UI shows required vs held (c1b 78/75). (2) Every NPC has a `smalltalk` branch that costs nothing and teaches nothing mechanical - that is deliberate; it is how you learn the voice, and it makes the gated lines feel earned. (3) Every NPC has a hostile branch, because being able to tell someone to get stuffed is the cheapest way to make a world feel real, and it has a real standing cost. (4) Night interactions exist only at the Low Lantern - the shift ends and people say what they actually think.

actors.description: Ferrymaster of the Patience. Sixty years old, forty of them on this river. She talks to the tide-post more than she talks to you.

day1.text: She looks you over the way you would look over a rope you were thinking of trusting. 'You're the new hand. Six tallies a day, two back for your bunk and your dinner, and you don't touch the fare box. Dawn, midday, dusk. Between crossings you're your own problem.' She turns back to the water. 'Tide-post reads the same as yesterday. That's eleven days now.'

eleven_days.text: 'Of nothing. That's the trouble.' She taps the post. 'Tide comes in, tide goes out, six hours each, and it has been doing that since before there was a river to do it in. Eleven days ago it started stopping. Sits at slack an hour longer each day.' She shrugs, and the shrug is not casual. 'Everyone says drift. I have been on this water forty years. It is not drift.'

choices.text: 'What happens if it stops turning altogether?'
Let her get back to it.

what_is_it.text: 'If I knew I'd have said.' A pause. 'Ask Fen. He was a salvager before his nerve went and he knows this water's bones. He'll be at the Lantern tonight, same as every night.' She glances at you. 'And listen on the crossings. People talk on the water. They think the engine noise covers it. It does not.'

full_slack.text: 'Then the Patience doesn't run, and I don't pay you, and neither of us eats.' She says it flatly. 'One day of full slack and this river is a dead thing with a town on each side of it.'

haggle.text: 'Six is what the last hand got, and he could splice.' She does not look up. 'Learn the work, hold a line in weather, and we'll talk on the seventh day. Ask me before then and I'll take it as notice.'

hub.text: She is doing something to a cleat with a marlinspike. 'Hand.'

choices.text: Tell her what you have worked out.

smalltalk.text: 'The day is the day.' She works the spike. 'Wind's southerly, which means the smell of the tannery, which means Doss will complain about the smell of the tannery, which means I will hear about the tannery for six hours.' She almost smiles. 'That's the day.'

work.text: 'Rope wants coiling, fares want taking, and the fenders want checking before the dusk run. Same as it was. Same as it will be.' She jerks her chin at the boat. 'Go on.'

mortgage.text: Her hands stop. She does not look up for a long moment. 'Who told you that.' It is not a question. 'Tally & Prewitt hold the paper on this boat and have held it nine years, and in nine years I have never once been late.' Now she looks up. 'Month's end. Yes. Is that what you wanted?'

choices.text: 'I wanted to know if it was true.'
'It might be worth something to somebody.'

mortgage_mercy.text: 'No,' she agrees. 'You're not.' She goes back to the cleat. After a while: 'She will offer you money for it. Prewitt. She offers everyone money for everything.' The spike turns. 'Forty years, hand. If this boat goes, I do not go anywhere. I just stop.'

mortgage_candor.text: 'It's true.' She resumes work. 'Truth is cheap on this river. It is what people do with it that costs.'

mortgage_threat.text: She sets the spike down very carefully, which is worse than throwing it. 'Get off my boat for the day.' Quiet. Even. 'Come back at dusk, do your work, and we will not speak of this again. But you have told me what you are, and I will not forget it.'

report.text: She listens without interrupting, which is not the same as agreeing. At the end she is quiet a while. 'Keep it in your head and off your tongue. This river runs on who owes who. The moment you are a hand who knows things, you stop being a hand who coils rope.'

quit.text: She puts the spike down. 'Say it plain. Are you walking off my boat?'

quit_yes.text: 'Then you're walking.' She holds out a hand, and her grip is dry and hard. 'Wage to today. No hard words. This river takes people off boats all the time and mostly they do not come back to say so.' She turns away. 'Don't drown. It's a poor way round.'

actors.description: Tally House agent. Young, badly slept, and holding something in that is heavier than he is.
actors._design: The worked example of the core mechanic. Every answer is offered as TEXT - you can always say it. It only WORKS at reliability. Calling it right cracks him open (+10 to the token, candor +1); bluffing costs candor and closes him for the day. His brother drowned in the Stairs, which is the mercy route into everything he knows.

hub.text: He is copying a column of figures and has copied the same line twice. 'Yes? The desk is Prewitt's. If it's business it's hers.'

choices.text: 'You look like a man who's been paid to forget something.'

smalltalk.text: 'Long month.' He rubs his eyes with the back of a wrist, ink and all, and now there is ink on his face and he does not know it. 'I came here to count. That's all I wanted to do, honestly - count things, go home. Nobody tells you the counting is the least of it.'

sluice.text: He does not look up, and the not-looking-up is the whole answer. 'The sluice closes itself. Nobody's touched it. It's a mechanism. It does what mechanisms do.'

choices.text: 'Men paid in Tally coin close it at the third bell.'
'The Weirkeeper closes it with her own hands.'
'Nothing touches it. It closes on its own, humming.'

bluffed.text: He looks up properly for the first time, and you can see him decide you are guessing. 'No,' he says, and the relief in it is insulting. 'No, you don't know that. You heard it at the Lantern and thought you'd try it on me.' He goes back to his column. 'Come back when you've got something. Or don't.'

needle.text: 'Get out.' He stands, and he is shaking, and it is not fear. 'You think you're the first? People come in here twice a week to tell me what I look like. I know what I look like. I have a mirror and a conscience and both are in better repair than you'd think.' He points at the door. 'Out.'

called_it.text: The pen stops. A blot spreads on the ledger and he watches it spread. 'You've seen the log.' It comes out of him all at once, low and fast: 'Four of them. They come down the Marl side at the second bell and they are gone by the fourth, and they are paid out of a chit I write myself. I write it. I have written it eleven times.' He puts both hands flat on the desk. 'I did not know what it was for. I want that said. I did not know.'

called_it_a.text: He blinks. 'Doon? The Weirkeeper?' Genuine confusion, and then something worse - relief. 'That would - yes. That would make more sense than what I have been telling myself.' He lets out a breath. 'She has the only hands on that gate. If it is her, then it is not us, and I would very much like it not to be us.'

called_it_c.text: For the first time he looks straight at you. 'You've heard it too.' His voice drops. 'I stayed late on the ninth. I heard the sluice go over and there was nobody on the walk, and it was not a machine sound. Machines don't hold a note.' He swallows. 'I have not said that to anyone, because saying it makes me the sort of man who says that sort of thing.'

chit.text: 'I can't - ' He stops. He looks at the door. Then he tears the top sheet off his blotter, folds it once, and pushes it across without letting go a second longer than he has to. 'That's a copy. I made it on the ninth because I was frightened. If Prewitt asks, you took it.'

who_pays.text: 'The chit comes down from the desk.' He does not say her name. He looks at the desk, which is Prewitt's, and he does not say her name, and that is him saying it. 'I write what the desk sends down. That's the job. That's all of the job.'

stop_writing.text: 'And then what?' Not angry. Tired. 'Then someone else writes it, and I am in the river, and the chit still gets written.' He picks the pen back up. 'You have been here a fortnight. I have been here four years. Don't tell me what to stop doing.'

brother.text: 'Who told you about Tam.' Flat. Then, because you clearly already know: 'He went down the Salt Steps on a salvage pull when I was nine. They brought up his hat.' He sets the pen down. 'That is why I took a desk job on a river I hate. So there would be one Ashe who died of a chest cold.'

choices.text: 'Then help me stop it happening to someone else.'

brother_mercy.text: The quiet goes on long enough to be uncomfortable and then long enough to be something else. 'Nobody waits,' he says eventually. 'They say the sorry and then they move it along.' He wipes his face, finds the ink, stares at his hand. 'The hum. On the ninth. You should know that I heard it, and you should know that I have been pretending I didn't, and I would like one person on this river to know both of those things.'

brother_lever.text: He looks at you with an expression that is almost admiring and entirely cold. 'There it is.' He nods slowly. 'You waited a whole four seconds before you made him useful.' He turns back to the ledger. 'Everyone on this river is a lever to somebody. I had hoped to reach the end of the week before I was one to you.'

actors.description: Your fellow deckhand. Talks constantly, works rarely, and knows every version of every story - including the wrong ones.
actors._design: A rumor mill. Doss carries EVERY answer to every triad at reliability 25, true or false, which is where false rumors come from. He is never lying on purpose. He is the reason a low-reliability journal is dangerous rather than empty.

hub.text: Doss has arranged the rope into something that is not a coil and is watching the bank go past. 'There you are. Tell me something. Anything. I've been out here with my own thoughts for an hour and they've started repeating.'

smalltalk.text: 'My day.' He considers it seriously, which is the joke. 'I woke up. The tide didn't. We're both dealing with it in our own way.' He nods at the water. 'Nine days ago I could tell you the hour from the smell of that bank. Now it smells like four in the afternoon at every hour God sends. It's unsettling, is what it is.'

rumor_mill.text: 'Everything. That's the trouble with what they're saying - they're saying all of it.' He starts counting off on his fingers, entirely cheerful. 'It's the Weirkeeper gone strange up there alone. It's the Tally House paying men to hold the gate shut for the barge trade. It's nobody at all and the river's just decided, which is my favourite, because it means nobody has to do anything.'

believes.text: 'Me? None of it. All of it.' He shrugs expansively. 'I'm a deckhand, mate. Believing things is for people with somewhere to be.' Then, a little quieter: 'I'll say this. Whichever one's true, somebody on this river already knows, and they've been very quiet about it for eleven days. That's the bit that gets me at night.'

sources.text: 'Ma Cobb, mostly. Passengers. You'd be amazed what people say six feet from a man coiling rope - it's like we're furniture.' He grins. 'Which, to be fair, on a good day I am.'

skim_accuse.text: The grin goes out like a lamp. He glances at the wheelhouse, then back. 'Keep your voice down.' A beat. 'A tenth. Off the Marl run only, and only when it's over twenty, and I've never once touched it on a thin day.' He is not really defending himself; he is reciting rules he made up to sleep at night. 'What do you want?'

choices.text: 'Nothing. I just wanted you to know I know.'

skim_join.text: Relief, and under it something that looks a lot like disappointment. 'Right. Right, yes.' He works out a share on his fingers. 'Marl run, over twenty, a tenth, split. Don't get clever and don't get greedy and for God's sake don't do it on a day she's counting.'

skim_stop.text: 'You'd do it, too.' He says it wonderingly, not angrily. 'All right. All right, it's stopped.' He puts the rope down and actually coils it. 'For what it's worth - and it isn't worth much - it was for my mother's rent, and that's the most boring possible reason, and I'd have preferred a better one.'

skim_hold.text: He looks at you for a long moment. 'That's worse, you know. That's much worse than telling her.' He picks the rope back up. 'Now I've got to be nice to you forever.' He says it lightly. He means it entirely.

nag.text: 'I am working. This is working.' He gestures at the rope, which is worse than when he started. 'Vigilance, this is. Someone's got to watch the water in case it does something.' He watches the water. It does nothing. 'See? Working.'

actors.description: Old salvager. Went down the Stairs for thirty years, stopped four years ago, and will not say why in daylight.
actors._design: The lore road, and the reason the tavern exists. Fen is reachable ONLY at night - the shift has to end before the deep history opens. Drink is the gate: each round raises what he will say by one tier, and the third round is where the Turning Words come out, sung, at reliability 30 - deliberately not enough. They must be corroborated elsewhere.

hub.text: Fen has the corner seat, the one with its back to two walls, and an empty cup he is turning slowly by the rim. He looks up without moving his head. 'Ferry hand. Sit or don't.'

choices.text: 'Hesper says you know this water's bones.'

smalltalk.text: 'Evening.' He turns the cup. 'Cobb's fire's drawing badly. It's the wind in the chimney, which is the wind off the Reach, which is the wind that hasn't shifted in eleven days.' A pause. 'Everything comes back to it. You'll notice that. Everything in this room comes back to it and not one man here will say so out loud.'

steps.text: 'Dry an hour at dawn ebb and an hour at dusk ebb, drowned the rest, and the hour is not a suggestion.' He sets the cup down. 'I have seen a man do the sums wrong by ten minutes. We did not get him back. The water doesn't come in like a wave. It comes in like a decision.'

bones.text: 'Did she.' He almost smiles. 'Hesper Quillon has been calling me an old fool for thirty years and I have been one for about twenty-eight of them, so she's ahead.' The smile goes. 'The bones, then. The Weir holds the tide. The tide holds the Stairs down. Something has got hold of the Weir. That is the bones, and all the rest is furniture.'

insult.text: The cup stops turning. The room does not go quiet - taverns don't - but the three men at the next table stop pretending not to listen. 'My nerve,' Fen says, 'went where it went because I used it up. Which is more than anyone has ever been able to say of yours.' He stands. He is old, and he is still a foot of shoulder wider than you. 'Now. Do you want to find out what's left of it, or do you want to sit down?'

choices.text: Sit down. 'That was out of order.'

apologise.text: He sits. It takes him a moment. 'It was.' He gets the cup turning again. 'But you said it to my face, which is where the others don't.' He does not look at you. 'Buy a round sometime.'

brawl.text: It lasts four seconds. He puts you into the settle with one flat shove of a hand that hauled wet cable for thirty years, and Ma Cobb is over the bar before you land, and that is the end of it. 'OUT,' says Cobb. 'Both - no. Not you, Fen. Sit down, Fen. YOU. Out.' From the floor, Fen looks almost sorry. He does not help you up.

round.text: He watches Cobb fill it and does not thank you, which from Fen is a kind of manners. 'You want something. That's fine. Everyone wants something, and most of them don't buy first.' He drinks. 'Ask.'

choices.text: 'What is it you sing when you're drunk?'

drink_quiet.text: You sit. He turns the cup. The fire draws badly. After a while he says, 'Most people talk,' and does not elaborate, and somehow it is the friendliest thing anyone has said to you all week.

stopped.text: A long silence. 'Four years ago I was down the Arcade at slack, pulling brass off a shopfront.' He is not looking at anything in this room. 'And I heard my own name. Under the water. In my mother's voice, and my mother had been dead since I was twenty.' He drinks. 'The wights plead. That is what they do. They plead in a voice you will follow.' He sets the cup down empty. 'I nearly went. That's all of the story. I nearly went, and I have not trusted my own ears since, and a salvager who cannot trust his ears is a corpse on a delay.'

undercity.text: 'A city. Not ruins - a city.' He leans in. 'Shopfronts with the numbers still on the doors. A cistern the size of a church. They had bells down there, great bronze things, and they rang them at the turn of every tide for four hundred years.' He turns the cup. 'Then one day the sea came over the top of them, and they went on ringing a while, and then they stopped. Nobody knows why the sea came. Nobody down there was ever asked.'

words.text: He is drunk enough now that the question amuses him. 'Sing? I don't sing.' And then, two minutes later, entirely unprompted, into his cup, half a bar of something in a cracked baritone: 'Ebb and hold and turn her round, three words at the third bell's sound...' He stops. He looks at you. 'That's nothing. That's a kiddie's rhyme. Cobb hums it at the bar and Wenna's lot chant it out on the rocks and it doesn't mean a thing.'

choices.text: Let him think you didn't notice.

words_let_go.text: You let it go. He relaxes by a degree so small only a man watching for it would see it, and turns the cup, and hums the rest of the bar without knowing he is doing it.

words_press.text: 'Then go and ask someone who'd know.' He pushes the cup away. 'Cobb has the rhyme whole. The hermit on the Rocks knows what it's for. And the third word is cut into the plaque at the Lesser Gate, where I am not going, and where you should not go either.' He stands, unsteadily. 'I have said more tonight than I have in a year. That's your two tallies' worth and a good deal over.'

actors.description: Head clerk and information broker. Perfectly courteous, perfectly incurious about your feelings, and the only person on the Reach who pays cash for a thing you merely know.
actors._design: The information market, and the hardest ongoing choice in the game. Price = base(category) x reliability x scarcity x Slack inflation. Every sale raises that token's SPREAD: later buyers pay less and the token starts appearing in NPC mouths, weakening it as leverage. Selling a secret about a named person ALERTS them. Hoard or sell is never obvious.

hub.text: She finishes her line, blots it, and only then looks up - and her attention, when it arrives, is complete and slightly alarming. 'The ferry hand. Sit down. You have the face of someone carrying something they haven't decided what to do with.'

choices.text: 'You hold the paper on the Patience.'
'Your man Corvin writes the sluice chits.'

smalltalk.text: 'Business is excellent, which is an unkind thing to say in a month like this one, so I shall say it quietly.' She caps the ink. 'When a river stops, everyone needs to know why, nobody can agree, and people who cannot agree will pay to be certain. I sell certainty. It is a better trade than grain and it does not spoil.' A small, dry smile. 'It does, actually. Rather fast. But it doesn't smell.'

market.text: 'I buy what is true and provable, and I pay less for what is merely going around.' She sets out a small brass scale, apparently for effect. 'Four rules and I will not bend them. Hearsay under half-certain fetches half price. The second person to sell me a thing gets less than the first. The tenth gets nothing, because by then it is weather, not news.' She folds her hands. 'And if you sell me something about a particular person, that person will eventually learn that someone sold it. Not from me. But they will.'

sell.text: 'Let's hear it.' She does not pick up the pen, which means she is listening properly.

mortgage.text: 'I hold the paper on eleven boats, four warehouses and a lighthouse the Crown believes it owns.' No defensiveness whatever. 'Hesper Quillon has never missed a payment in nine years and I expect she will not miss this one. If she does, I shall take the boat, and I shall feel nothing about it, and that is precisely why I am good at this and she is not.'

choices.text: 'Would you take an extension? From me?'

extension.text: For the first time she looks genuinely interested. 'From you. A deckhand.' She considers it exactly as seriously as a business proposition deserves. 'Thirty tallies buys her a fortnight. Sixty buys her the quarter. I shall not discount it for sentiment, and I shall not tell her where it came from unless you wish me to.' She picks the pen back up. 'People are very strange about being helped.'

cold.text: 'It is.' She agrees so readily that it takes the wind out of it. 'I was a bargeman's daughter on the Far Wend side, and I watched my father lose everything twice to men who felt a great deal and paid nothing. Feeling is not the opposite of taking your boat. It is usually the preface.' Back to the ledger. 'Was there anything else?'

confront.text: She reads the copied chit without hurrying, top to bottom, twice. Then she sets it down on the desk between you, squared to the edge. 'Yes,' she says. 'That is our chit, that is our money, and those are our men.' She meets your eyes. 'Now. You may sell it to the Wardens, who will convene an Assize and take four days about it. You may sell it back to me, for rather more than they will pay. Or you may do neither, and keep it, and we shall both know that you have it.' A pause. 'I would think carefully. The third is worth the most and pays nothing at all.'

buy_back.text: 'Forty.' Instantly, without haggling, which tells you it is worth a great deal more. 'And I shall add something you cannot buy: the men on that crew are not ours. They are hired through a factor in Far Wend, and I do not know who instructs the factor.' She slides the coins across. 'That is not a deflection. I genuinely do not know, and it has been keeping me awake.'

thin.text: She glances at the page and hands it straight back. 'That is a copy of a copy, it is not initialled, and a clerk having a bad week could have written it in an hour.' Not unkind. 'Bring me the thing itself, or bring me the man who wrote it and have him say so aloud. Then we shall talk about money.'

to_assize.text: 'Then take it to the Assize.' She squares the papers on her desk. 'I shall be there, and I shall bring the factor's contract, and we shall discover together who has been instructing whom.' She almost smiles. 'You may find I am on your side of that room. It would not be the first time I have been mistaken for the villain by people who had not finished reading.'

hold.text: 'Sensible.' She returns to her ledger, and the interview is plainly over. 'Do remember that paper rots, hand, and that a man who has been frightened for eleven days becomes a man who is frightened for twelve.' The pen resumes. 'Whatever you mean to do with it, do it this week.'
